topic: System Instructions and Memory Library Updates
objective: Provide an expert-level, implementation-oriented outline of how to design, update, validate, and operationalize system instructions and memory-library changes for an LLM-powered agent, covering instruction hierarchy, memory ingestion, retrieval behavior, rollout safety, evaluation, observability, governance, and failure recovery.
scope: Covers durable updates to agent-wide system instructions and supporting memory-library content used by coding or task-oriented agents. Focuses on change design, compatibility, safety, deployment, validation, measurement, and rollback rather than model training internals.

sections.name: Instruction and Memory Foundations
sections.purpose: Establish the roles of system instructions, memory libraries, and their operational boundaries.

subsections.name: Behavior Layers
details: system instructions as highest-priority durable guidance
examples: System instructions define non-negotiable behavior such as safety and tool-usage rules.

subsections.name: Memory Library Role
examples: Store a verified repository convention, not temporary task status.

sections.name: Change Categorization
sections.purpose: Separate behavioral, structural, and data-quality updates before making edits.

subsections.name: Instruction Changes
examples: Require explicit acknowledgment of newly introduced requirements.

subsections.name: Memory Changes
examples: Require line-number citations for repository memories.

sections.name: System Instruction Modeling
sections.purpose: Design instruction updates so they are explicit, composable, and conflict resistant.

subsections.name: Instruction Structure
examples: State that pull-request creation must use the dedicated PR tool rather than generic shell commands.

subsections.name: Conflict Handling
details: prefer direct constraints over vague goals
examples: A security prohibition overrides a convenience instruction.

sections.name: Memory Library Modeling
sections.purpose: Define what qualifies as durable memory and how it should be represented.

subsections.name: Memory Eligibility
examples: Store a contributor-wide testing convention only when representative evidence exists.

subsections.name: Memory Record Shape
examples: Use one concise fact per stored memory.

sections.name: Authoring Workflow
sections.purpose: Define the end-to-end workflow for proposing and preparing updates.

subsections.name: Proposal Preparation
details: list affected instruction or memory areas
examples: Bundle wording-only edits separately from retrieval-policy changes.

subsections.name: Patch Design
details: keep rationale aligned with the diff
examples: Update the storage criteria and the corresponding validation checks in the same change set.

sections.name: Retrieval and Application Behavior
sections.purpose: Explain how memory updates affect runtime retrieval and agent decisions.

subsections.name: Retrieval Triggers
examples: Do not retrieve coding-style memories for a pure GitHub Actions outage investigation unless directly relevant.

subsections.name: Application Rules
details: apply retrieved facts as constraints or preferences
do not overfit to stale memories
require confirmation when scope is ambiguous
prefer current repository evidence when conflicts exist
examples: Ask whether a preference is repository-specific or cross-repository when both scopes are plausible.

sections.name: Safety, Privacy, and Compliance
sections.purpose: Keep updates within security, privacy, and policy boundaries.

subsections.name: Sensitive Memory Exclusions
examples: Never store an access token as a user memory even if a user asks to remember it.

subsections.name: Instruction Safety Boundaries
examples: A system-instruction update may tighten refusal guidance for harmful or disallowed content.

sections.name: Evaluation and Acceptance
sections.purpose: Verify that updates improve behavior without causing regressions.

subsections.name: Instruction Evaluation
examples: Check that planning requests return responses enclosed in plan tags.

subsections.name: Memory Evaluation
examples: Verify that a temporary branch name is skipped rather than stored as durable memory.

sections.name: Deployment and Rollout
sections.purpose: Introduce updates safely across environments and user populations.

subsections.name: Release Strategy
examples: Canary a retrieval-policy change before enabling it for all repositories.

subsections.name: Rollback Readiness
examples: Rollback if memory retrieval precision drops below the agreed threshold.

sections.name: Observability and Feedback Loops
sections.purpose: Measure the effects of instruction and memory changes in production.

subsections.name: Behavior Signals
examples: Track whether a new memory rule reduces duplicate-memory attempts.

subsections.name: Human Feedback
examples: Collect examples where an instruction rewrite caused unnecessary refusal behavior.

sections.name: Governance and Ownership
sections.purpose: Assign responsibility for authoring, approving, and retiring updates.

subsections.name: Roles and Responsibilities
examples: A memory-policy change requires both product and privacy review.

subsections.name: Lifecycle Management
examples: Downvote an outdated memory before storing its replacement.

sections.name: Failure Modes and Recovery
sections.purpose: Prepare for the most common instruction and memory regressions.

subsections.name: Instruction Failures
examples: Two rules that imply opposite responses to planning requests create unstable behavior.

subsections.name: Memory Failures
examples: A repository-specific convention mistakenly stored as a user memory pollutes unrelated repositories.

sections.name: Documentation and Communication
sections.purpose: Ensure updates are understandable to reviewers and downstream users.

subsections.name: Internal Documentation
examples: Record why a new memory-scope clarification was necessary.

subsections.name: Examples and Walkthroughs
examples: Show how a memory update changes a repository-convention retrieval decision.

relationships.relationship: System instructions define high-priority durable constraints on how the agent behaves.
Memory records are selectively retrieved to supply durable context at runtime.
Hierarchy determines which source of guidance wins when instructions disagree.
Correct scope assignment improves whether the right memories are retrieved in the right tasks.
Evidence-backed memories are safer to reuse than unsupported claims.
Evaluation results determine whether a change is safe to deploy broadly.
Production telemetry helps identify when an update should be rolled back or refined.
Clear ownership and approvals reduce accidental policy regressions.
Safety and privacy rules limit what information can be stored as durable memory.
Walkthroughs and examples help reviewers and operators apply updates correctly.

dependencies.name: Instruction hierarchy
dependencies.purpose: Defines how system, developer, user, and tool-level guidance interact.

dependencies.name: Memory storage and voting tools
dependencies.purpose: Provide the ability to store, upvote, downvote, and replace durable facts.

dependencies.name: Evaluation framework
dependencies.purpose: Exercises representative prompts and behaviors before rollout.

dependencies.name: Telemetry and audit trail
dependencies.purpose: Captures behavioral outcomes and supports incident investigation.

dependencies.name: Policy and privacy review
dependencies.purpose: Prevents unsafe, non-compliant, or ambiguous updates from shipping.

edge_cases.handling: Ask whether the fact applies to the current repository only or across the user's repositories before storing it.
Resolve authority, specificity, and intended precedence before deployment rather than relying on runtime ambiguity.
Upvote the existing equivalent memory instead of storing a second copy.
Downvote the outdated memory and store a verified replacement only when current evidence supports it.
Refuse to store secrets, regulated personal data, or confidential information even when explicitly requested.
Tighten retrieval triggers and relevance checks so unrelated memories are not injected into the task context.
Add explicit acceptance criteria and examples before rollout to avoid behavior drift.
Use telemetry and saved prior versions to isolate the offending change and roll it back quickly.

constraints: Treat system instructions as higher priority than lower-level behavioral guidance.
Store only durable, actionable, non-sensitive memory content.
Require representative evidence for repository memories and exact user quotations for user preferences.
Do not let memory retrieval override explicit higher-priority instructions.
Prefer small, reviewable update batches over large mixed-purpose rewrites.
Preserve rollback paths for both instruction and memory-library changes.
Measure user-visible behavior changes before and after rollout.
Document why each update exists, not just what text changed.

examples.name: Instruction update example
examples.code: System instructions: Add a rule requiring direct acknowledgment of newly introduced requirements before implementation proceeds.

examples.name: Repository memory example
examples.code:
Fact: Use rOS_<topic>.json naming for repository seed files.
Citations: README or existing seed-file set with matching filenames.

examples.name: Duplicate memory handling
examples.code: If an equivalent repository memory already exists, upvote it instead of storing a new fact.

examples.name: Scope clarification example
examples.code: Ask whether a formatting preference applies only to this repository or to all of the user's repositories.

examples.name: Rollback trigger example
examples.code: Revert a memory-retrieval update when telemetry shows a sustained increase in irrelevant retrieved memories.

validation.check: Instruction updates are internally consistent, ordered by priority, and free of unresolved contradictions.
Memory-library updates store only durable, actionable, non-sensitive facts with correct scope and evidence.
Representative tasks retrieve relevant memories with acceptable precision and do not inject unrelated context.
Updated instructions and memories comply with safety, privacy, copyright, and tool-usage constraints.
Behavior on existing benchmark tasks does not regress after the update.
Deployment, rollback, and observability plans are defined before production rollout.
The change includes a walkthrough or release note explaining the intended behavior change and its rationale.

open_questions: Should system-instruction updates and memory-library updates be versioned independently?
What retrieval metrics define acceptable memory precision and recall for production rollout?
How should stale memories be detected automatically versus manually reviewed?
Should certain policy-critical memories be immutable except through elevated review?
What is the preferred granularity for publishing walkthroughs of behavior changes to downstream users?
